query: For Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 initially in a high-temperature BCC state, the factors governing its phase stability during cooling and subsequent thermal exposure are not understood well enough to account for the range of phases that may appear. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain this behavior and why? Define a controlled comparison and baseline, predicted observations relative to that baseline, the conditions under which the hypothesis should and should not apply, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification result.

generation.hypothesis: In Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7, the kinetics of short-range ordering (SRO) during cooling control the phase transformations from the high‐temperature BCC state. A slow cooling rate promotes the development of SRO clusters that act as nucleation sites for secondary phase formation, while rapid quenching suppresses SRO, maintaining the metastable BCC structure.
generation.material_initial_state: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 in a high-temperature single-phase BCC state
generation.intervention: Tailor the cooling route by comparing rapid quenching versus controlled slow cooling from the high-temperature state
generation.conditions: This mechanism is expected to operate during the cooling process from high temperature and subsequent moderate thermal exposures that permit SRO evolution. It may not apply during re-heating to high temperatures or in cases where the alloy’s composition limits SRO development.
generation.structural_mediator: Short-range order (SRO) clusters of transition metal atoms (and aluminum) that form during slow cooling
generation.mechanism: During slow cooling, sufficient time is provided for atomic rearrangements that form SRO clusters. These clusters lower the local free energy barriers and serve as nucleation sites for secondary phase precipitates. In contrast, rapid quenching freezes the high-temperature configuration and minimizes SRO, thereby preserving the BCC phase.
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples that are slow cooled will show evidence of emerging secondary phases (e.g., additional diffraction peaks or distinct microstructural features indicative of phase separation) relative to rapidly quenched samples, which are expected to remain primarily BCC.
generation.baseline: A rapidly quenched Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 sample that retains a uniform BCC microstructure with minimal detectable SRO and no (or minimal) secondary phase formation.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis specifically applies when the alloy composition and thermal exposure conditions allow for significant SRO development. It may not hold if, for instance, the atomic interactions in the alloy do not favor SRO or if the imposed thermal history does not provide enough time for ordering processes to occur.
generation.uncertainty: While the general trend is anticipated, the precise nature and extent of the secondary phases, and the kinetics of SRO under varied cooling conditions, remain to be quantified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 samples from the high-temperature BCC state. One group is subjected to rapid quenching to room temperature, while the other is slowly cooled under controlled conditions. Follow both treatments with identical thermal exposures at an intermediate temperature to allow any transformation kinetics to play out.
measurements: X-ray diffraction (XRD) to detect additional phase peaks and assess phase purity
Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to image microstructural differences and secondary phase formation
Atom probe tomography (APT) to detect any SRO clusters and compositional variations
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the slow-cooled samples do not exhibit statistically significant differences in phase composition, microstructure, or the presence of secondary phases relative to the quenched samples, then the hypothesis that cooling rate-dependent SRO drives phase transformation in this alloy is falsified.

Such small precipitates are also found in the solution-annealed state of the Al3.31Co27.27Cr18.18Fe18.18Ni27.27Ti5.78 alloy []. This rapid formation may be indicative of short-range ordering (SRO) effects present, particularly between Ni and Ti, as these small particles already have high concentrations of these elements. It can be assumed that SRO may serve as a precursor for long-range ordered precipitates (LRO) formed during quenching and subsequent tempering []. According to Owen et al. [], SRO can be distinguished between statistical and microdomain types of SRO. The authors assume that with cooling from the solution annealing temperature, at first, a statistical SRO and then micro-domain SRO is present as a precursor phase, leading to the immediate formation of long-range ordered (Ni,Co)3(Ti,Al) precipitates. In this work, the aging behavior of a promising CCA for high-temperature application from WQ state to a maximum of 50 h aging at 750 °C is characterized by SEM, TEM, and APT measurements. The shape, size, and composition of the matrix and precipitate phases are determined and compared to Ni-based superalloys from the literature. Properties of individual phases have been studied using ab-initio-based model calculations supported by complementary experimental investigations. The following conclusions can be drawn from the results: After 10 h of aging at 750 °C, the majority of the thermodynamically stable γ’ ((Ni,Co)3(Al,Ti)) precipitates are formed. A comparison of the precipitate size after 50 h of aging with state-of-the-art Ni-based alloys from the literature suggests a comparatively low coarsening of the particles. Ni- and Ti-rich precipitates are observed in APT measurements of the WQ state, which already possess the stoichiometric ratio of the (Ni,Co)3(Al,Ti) γ’ phase. This indicates that it is nearly impossible to obtain a fully supersaturated and single-phased (ideal HEA) state in the selected CCA. More recently, long-term annealing experiments at intermediate temperatures revealed that different crystalline phases could precipitate out of the CoCrFeMnNi HEA fcc matrix. Moreover, finite-temperature ab initio simulation results suggest that the free energy of the hcp (hexagonal-close-packing) crystallographic lattice in the CoCrFeMnNi HEA may be lowest at room temperature, compared with that of its bcc (body-centerd-cubic) and fcc counterparts. All these results cast doubt on the high structural stability of HEA lattices, which is obviously a critical and vital problem for our understanding and applications of these newly developed metallic materials and multicomponent oxides. However, until now the predicted hcp phase of the CoCrFeMnNi HEA has not been observed in any experiments and the question of viable polymorphism remains unanswered.

reading.lever: Tailor cooling rates to modulate SRO-driven phase transformations.
reading.why: This approach, proven in similar HEA and non-equiatomic systems, directly tests if cooling history induces the microstructural changes observed in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7.
